limitations: The supplied rule has no clause of the form if(value == null), no condition(...) runtime predicate, and no special-case rule-language treatment for a null KeyStore.
The rule contains no AspectJ target(T) or args(T) matcher, so it does not itself state a subtype-matching condition.
The meanings and interprocedural recognition rules for generatedKeyStore, generatedManagerFactoryParameters, and notHardCoded are not defined in this CrySL file.
A warning about absent abstract provenance is not runtime evidence about an argument's value, loading state, contents, or provider treatment.
The representative null-KeyStore message is not entailed by an explicit null-related clause in the reproduced rule; any such interpretation requires detector behavior or evidence beyond this rule.
predicates: generatedKeyStore[keyStore] is required for init(keyStore, password).
neverTypeOf[password, java.lang.String] and notHardCoded[password] constrain the password object used by init(keyStore, password).
algorithm in {"PKIX", "SunX509"} constrains both getInstance event alternatives.
generatedKeyManager[this] is ensured after either Init alternative.
detector_semantics.claim: The rule defines the event language Get, Init, GetKeyMng? with ORDER Get, Init, GetKeyMng?, together with its listed algorithm/password constraints, required abstract predicates, and ensured abstract predicates.

unknowns: Whether the detector that produced the representative warning implements null-specific behavior beyond the reproduced CrySL rule.
The formal analysis semantics of generatedKeyStore, generatedManagerFactoryParameters, neverTypeOf, and notHardCoded in the detector version used.
The selected provider and its exact null-KeyStore behavior in the affected runtime.
Whether the relevant key material is actually loaded, contains usable private-key entries and certificate chains, and is selected during TLS authentication.
Why the rule permits SunX509 while the current Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification names PKIX as the standard KeyManagerFactory algorithm.

documented_behavior: KeyManagerFactory is a factory for key managers based on key material sources.
getInstance selects an implementation from a supporting security provider; provider selection is runtime-dependent when no provider is explicitly named.
init(KeyStore, char[]) initializes from key material; its KeyStore parameter is documented as "the key store or null."
getKeyManagers() returns one key manager for each type of key material and throws IllegalStateException if the factory was not initialized.
preconditions: getInstance requires a non-null algorithm name.
The String-provider overload requires a non-null, non-empty provider name; the Provider overload requires a non-null Provider.
The API documents that the password is used to recover keys in the KeyStore; a wrong password can cause UnrecoverableKeyException.

A KeyStore normally must be loaded before it can be accessed, unless it was already loaded during instantiation; the exact interaction with a KeyManagerFactory implementation remains provider-specific.
unknowns: Java SE documentation does not specify what a particular provider does when init is called with a null KeyStore.
Java SE documentation does not define the CrySL abstract predicates generatedKeyStore or generatedManagerFactoryParameters.
The provider, provider ordering, configured default algorithm, supported provider-specific algorithms, and source of actual key material cannot be determined from this rule alone.

non_security_violation_shapes: Calling getKeyManagers() before initialization in diagnostic or dead code where the resulting IllegalStateException is handled and no key manager is used for TLS.
Creating and initializing a factory solely for a local test or capability probe with a hard-coded test password, where no production credential or TLS identity is involved.
Initializing with a locally constructed input that lacks the rule's generated* provenance predicate, where the resulting factory is never used to authenticate a peer or present a credential.

Using init(ManagerFactoryParameters) with an application-specific parameter object that the selected provider accepts, but which has no producer predicate recognized by this rule, in code with no security-sensitive use of the result.
important_note: This is a CrySL-style static rule for javax.net.ssl.KeyManagerFactory. It establishes only the stated call-order, value-constraint, and abstract-provenance predicates. It does not prove that a KeyStore was loaded, contains an appropriate private key and certificate chain, that a provider uses a particular default source, or that resulting managers are installed in and used by a TLS context. In particular, the reproduced rule does not contain a null-KeyStore condition.

events.condition: Matches getInstance(algorithm). The rule constrains algorithm to {"PKIX", "SunX509"}.
events.name: g1

events.condition: Matches getInstance(algorithm, _). The second argument is unconstrained by the rule; algorithm is constrained to {"PKIX", "SunX509"}.
events.name: g2

events.condition: Matches init(keyStore, password) on the governed factory. The rule requires generatedKeyStore[keyStore], neverTypeOf[password, java.lang.String], and notHardCoded[password]. It has no explicit null test or other runtime-value predicate for keyStore.
events.name: i1

events.condition: Matches init(params) on the governed factory. The rule requires generatedManagerFactoryParameters[params].
events.name: i2

events.condition: Matches keyManager = getKeyManagers(). ORDER permits it only after Get followed by Init; the rule ensures generatedKeyManagers[keyManager] after this event.
events.name: gkm1

security_semantics.runtime_claim: At runtime, KeyManagerFactory behavior depends on the selected provider and supplied values. In particular, a null KeyStore is API-permitted, while its semantics are provider-specific.
security_semantics.detector_claim: The rule enforces a narrow static policy: algorithm values restricted to PKIX or SunX509, a non-String and non-hard-coded password representation, recognized provenance of initialization inputs, and factory initialization before optional retrieval of managers.

compatibility: Confirm that the deployed provider supports the requested algorithm name.
Use PKIX when Java SE standard-name portability is required; treat SunX509 and other names as provider compatibility questions.
For ManagerFactoryParameters initialization, confirm that the selected provider accepts the concrete parameter implementation.
runtime: Identify the actual security provider and KeyManagerFactory implementation selected in the deployment.
For a null KeyStore, inspect that provider's documented or source-defined behavior and the actual source of key material.
Verify the selected key material, recoverability password, key-manager output, and whether those managers are passed to a TLS context and exercised.
source_level: Resolve the receiver as javax.net.ssl.KeyManagerFactory rather than a similarly named factory or a namesake type ending in Spec.
Establish the relevant getInstance, init, and getKeyManagers call order on the same factory object.
Trace the algorithm value, password representation and origin, and any producer evidence for the KeyStore or ManagerFactoryParameters argument.
For a null-related report, determine whether the warning is solely an unestablished generatedKeyStore predicate or relies on additional detector behavior outside the supplied rule.

forbidden_inferences_without_evidence: That a null KeyStore argument is prohibited by the Java API; init(KeyStore, char[]) documents its KeyStore parameter as "the key store or null."
That a null KeyStore necessarily selects a platform-default key source; Java SE leaves a provider's null-KeyStore behavior unspecified.
That failure to establish generatedKeyStore[keyStore] proves that no KeyStore was loaded or that its contents are insecure.
That successful KeyManagerFactory initialization proves the returned managers are later supplied to SSLContext.init or used in a completed TLS handshake.

That the rule's allowance of SunX509 makes it a current Java Security Standard Algorithm Name; the standard-names specification lists PKIX for KeyManagerFactory, while providers may support additional names.
That the rule checks certificate validity, key strength, key-manager alias selection, TLS protocol versions, cipher suites, peer authentication, or hostname verification.
name: KeyManagerFactorySpec
semantic_scope: For every finding of this rule, the detector observes the specified construction, initialization, and optional key-manager retrieval events on javax.net.ssl.KeyManagerFactory; restricts the requested algorithm to PKIX or SunX509; rejects a password represented as java.lang.String or considered hard-coded; and requires abstract producer predicates for the KeyStore or ManagerFactoryParameters argument. It does not directly observe provider internals, KeyStore contents, default-source loading, null-value semantics, or TLS-session behavior.
known_false_positive_shapes: A provider-supported and deployment-tested init(null, password) invocation reported only because the analyzer cannot establish generatedKeyStore[null]. Java SE permits a null KeyStore argument, while the rule has no corresponding exception.
A valid provider-specific KeyManagerFactory algorithm reported because it is not exactly PKIX or SunX509, despite Java SE permitting implementations to support additional algorithms.

A KeyStore or ManagerFactoryParameters object produced through a wrapper, library boundary, reflection, dependency injection, or unsupported interprocedural path that is semantically valid but not recognized as satisfying the rule's generated* predicate.
A runtime-derived char[] password incorrectly classified as hard-coded by the detector's value/provenance analysis.

detector_examples.message: a null KeyStore given to KeyManagerFactory.init requests the platform default key source, whose loading was not observed
